To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the current HEDIS performance measure fails to prioritize patients with the worst glycetic control and that it is feasible for safety-net clinics to analyze their diabetic patients by level of disease-control on the basis of changes in A1C over time.

the current performance measure for diabetes control in safety net populations fails to capture the most important patients for improvement, and that a performance measure based on the change in A1C over time can better identify patients for improvement and is feasible for safety nets.

1) patients with the worst glycemia control tend to have a larger improvement in A1c than other patients; 2) the current performance measure for diabetes control fails to identify patients who have the largest improvement in glycemic control; and 3) the new performance metric that we propose identifies patients who have the greatest reduction in glycemia control and may be more effective at improving diabetes outcomes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and evaluation of a new performance measure for diabetes control in safety net clinics that focuses on the patients at highest risk for complications.
a new approach to the measurement of the quality of care provided to patients with diabetes.
the development and application of new statistical methods for the analysis of longitudinal and clustered data.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

there was no evidence of any effect on the risk of cardiovascular events from the use of statins in the general population, or from the use of aspirin in patients without a prior history of cardiovascular disease.
there is insufficient evidence to recommend the use of a single performance measure to assess glycemic control among patients with diabetes.
the use of a performance measure that accounts for change in Alc over time may be a better indicator of quality improvement in diabetes control than a standard performance measure.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the current HEDIS measure for diabetes control is inadequate for safety-net patients and does not account for the most vulnerable patients.

the current performance measures fail to identify the patients with the greatest need for intervention, and that a performance measure derived from change in A1C over time would identify these patients and improve the care of this vulnerable population.
our results indicate that the current HEDIS measure for glycemic control does not accurately reflect the true performance of a safety net population with diabetes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is feasible to measure and track glycemic control in a safety net clinic setting.
it's possible to improve the performance measure to better reflect the population that needs to be targeted for improvement.
we need to focus more on those with the worst glycemia, who are often the ones that have the most room for improvement.
